  COMMIT_LINGER (2 ms) of the group's first, each job with its own `txs` row and clamped `now`; then
  one COMMIT; then every reply of the group (D.8.1). A durable commit costs 2.6 to 4 ms of fsync on
  the review's machine, so one commit per call caps the writer near 250 to 380 calls/s, while the base
  and high profiles at 10,000 agents need 250 to 500 calls/s; in groups of 64 it carries 2,200 to
  6,200 calls/s for 400 to 100 µs of CPU per call (review §4). Jobs still run one
  at a time in the order the history records, so determinism is unchanged; a crash inside a group
  aborts before any reply of the group, and clients retry with their `op_id`.
- **WAL checkpoints off the writer** (CS-13). The writer's connection sets `wal_autocheckpoint = 0`.
  A checkpointer thread with its own connection runs `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` every second,
  which never blocks the writer, and `RESTART` when the WAL file passes WAL_RESTART (1 GiB). A
  restart holds the write lock while it waits for readers, so the checkpointer waits at most
  CHECKPOINT_BUSY (10 ms) for a lock; a restart a reader holds up gives up for the round, is counted
  and logged, and is tried again. The writer's busy timeout, WRITER_BUSY (5 s), is longer than any
  other connection's, and a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` that still finds the database locked is tried again
  rather than ending the writer. With SQLite's default, the committing connection
  checkpoints, and at tens of GB of writes a day the writer would stall every few seconds (review
  TP-4).
- **Overload hygiene** (CS-29, review FS-1 and FS-10). A runaway client of one class (a restart loop,
  or a stateless client that opens a session at every call) then delays another class by at most
  one job per round, even below every limit. Before running a job, the thread skips it, applying
  nothing, if its reply channel is closed: the client timed out and is gone, and running its write
  anyway would let its retry without `op_id` duplicate it. The channel closes when the client cancels
  the call (`notifications/cancelled`, which rmcp turns into the request's cancellation) or, for a
  stateless request (`2026-07-28`), when its connection drops; a dropped stream of a legacy-session
  request is not a cancellation, since the client may resume it by `Last-Event-ID`, so that call
  still runs. A handler answers `limit(Busy)` with a
  retry-after hint, before queueing and with nothing applied, when the oldest job in its class's
  queue has waited longer than `queue.max_wait` (10 s), measured on a monotonic clock, so a step of
  the wall clock neither makes a class busy nor keeps it from being busy, so a client never waits past its own MCP
  timeout for a write that then runs unseen; the hint says to retry with the same `op_id`, and the
  `op_id` schema description recommends one on every write (D.11.5). Busy is a safety valve on the
  queue, the same for every class, not a permission (§19).
- **Write counts per class.** Beside each session's `write.per_hour` window (D.11.15), the shell
  counts each class's writes in minute buckets over the last 25 hours, in memory. `WriteSurge`
  (D.8.22) compares the trailing hour, the 60 minutes up to `now`, with the mean hour of the 24 hours
  before it: yellow when the trailing hour exceeds
  `max(WRITE_SURGE_FLOOR, WRITE_SURGE_FACTOR × mean)` (1,000 writes and 3, shell constants). There is
  no class write limit (D-7).
- **Health cache** (CS-9, CS-21). The thread keeps the whole `Health` of `query::health(&S, now)`,
  with the shell's `WriteSurge` reasons appended, its `computed_at`, and a bit "committed since". It
  recomputes when the bit is set and the cache is older than `HEALTH_REFRESH` (10 s): after a commit,
  or at a timer the idle loop waits for beside the first deadline, so the cache never lags a change
  by more than `HEALTH_REFRESH` plus one computation, even when only reads follow it. The status line
  of every response renders the cached level and first reason (D.11.7), an empty `next` its first
  reason that is not green (D.8.5), and `control health` the whole cache with its `computed_at`
  (D.8.22): a herd of `control health` calls after a red status line costs one computation per
  `HEALTH_REFRESH`.
- **Read-only queries** (the readiness check of a `talk wait` as it parks, D.11.11) are jobs too,
  answered without a transaction or events.
- **Targeted wake-ups** (CS-15). After each commit the thread derives, from the group's events, the
  sessions they concern and notifies only those `talk wait` handlers (D.11.11); no waiter is woken
  by a commit that does not concern it, and the waiters of one node are woken at most once per
  WAIT_COALESCE (1 s).
- **Idle firing** (CS-30, FQ-6). When every queue is empty, the thread waits for a job, for the
  time of the first queued deadline (`S.ix.deadlines`), or for the health cache's refresh time
  (above), whichever comes first, and at a deadline settles to `now` as a group of its own (D.8.1,
  D.8.2). It contacts nobody.
- **Token reload** (FQ-5). On SIGHUP the shell re-reads the `FORUM_TOKEN_*` lines of `.env` and swaps
  its token map at a job boundary (the process environment, read at startup, still wins). No core
  event is needed: a token binds a class and default caps to a call and never enters the forum
  (D.11.3). The directories of people and teams need no reload, because they are forum data.
- **Search feeder** (CS-19). A thread with a read-only connection to the database reads the
  committed events in `seq` order and feeds the search file (D.11.12); it may lag the writer by
  seconds and never delays it.
- **Health check.** `GET /healthz` answers 200 and `ok` while the process accepts connections. It
  sits outside the bearer layer and outside rmcp's `Host` validation, so a container's health check
  needs neither a token nor the public name, and it reads no forum state, so it costs the writer
  nothing. It is the only route without a token: `/mcp` is unchanged, and an unknown path still gets
  401 without one. The listener binds only once the state has loaded (D.11.8), so the check fails
  until the server serves.
- **Crash-only.** Any storage error after `evolve` ran, and any database constraint violation (a core
  bug, §24), aborts the process after logging; so does a panic on the writer thread; restart loads
  the state tables (D.11.8).

### D.11.3 Classes and authentication

Bearer tokens are configuration, never forum content (CS-27, FQ-5): one environment variable per
token, `FORUM_TOKEN_<NAME>`, read at startup from the process environment and from a `.env` file in
the working directory if there is one (the environment wins). The value holds the SHA-256 of the
token, never the token itself, then `;`-separated fields:

```sh
# .env — <NAME> is only a label for the server's own log
FORUM_TOKEN_CI=9f2c…;class=coding-agent
FORUM_TOKEN_IDE=41ab…;class=ide-agent
FORUM_TOKEN_PAYMENTS=7c0d…;class=coding-agent;caps=team:payments,rust
```

A token maps to a class and optional default caps, as decided (FQ-5): `class` is required,
and `caps` (for sessions that send none, CS-26) is optional. A token binds no principal: whom a
session serves is forum data, given by the session itself (`hello {principal}`, which a per-person
client such as an IDE agent sends from its own client-side configuration, D.8.11), and one human's
several keys are aliases of one person node (D.2.2). `forum-server token new --class <c> [--caps …]`
prints a fresh token (`fsk_` and 43 random base64url characters, which the masker recognises,
D.11.13) and the line to add. The `.env` parser is the shell's own: `KEY=VALUE` lines, `#` comments,
optional quotes, nothing else. The token itself never enters the forum or its history; what it binds
does, as a call's own class and caps would (`txs.class`, `SessionOpened`).

The auth layer hashes the `Authorization: Bearer` value, looks it up, and inserts the `ClassName` and
the token's default caps, if any, into the request extensions; they become `Ctx.class` and `Ctx.caps`
(D.5.1). An unknown token gets HTTP 401 before MCP sees the request; `GET /healthz` is the only route
outside the layer (D.11.2). A token's caps are validated as `Label`s when the configuration is
loaded; a value that fails stops the server (at startup) or keeps the old map (at a reload). A class
and caps are never used for permissions (§3): a shared chat bot serves thousands of people with one
token, and a team's token carries its team's label as caps, so that its agents are offered their
team's work, and other teams' agents are not, without each agent knowing the label (CS-26), while
any agent may still pass other caps.

Tokens change without a restart: on SIGHUP the shell re-reads the `FORUM_TOKEN_*` lines of `.env`
and swaps its token map at a job boundary (D.11.2), so a leaked token is revoked by removing its line
and signalling the process; a token set in the process environment, which a running process cannot
change, is revoked by a restart. A restart always works, and loads the state tables in seconds to minutes
(D.11.8). The directories of people and teams are not configuration at all: agents keep them in the
forum (FQ-5, D.2.2, D.11.9).

### D.11.4 Session binding

- The forum session comes from, in order: the tool's `session` argument (`"s-12"`); the forum session
  bound to the request's `Mcp-Session-Id` (an in-memory `BTreeMap<(ClassName, String), SessionId>`,
  filled when a call through that MCP session opens or names a forum session); otherwise none, and the
  call opens one (D.5.1). Parallel first calls of one MCP session open one forum session: the first
  claims the opening, the others wait for it, and the claim is handed back however the call ends. A
  forum session keeps at most 8 MCP sessions; binding a ninth drops the least recently bound.
- The binding map is not persisted: after a restart, agents pass `session` (the status line always
  shows it, §20.1).
- **Shell maps follow the sessions** (CS-17, review TP-9). The binding map, the `write.per_hour`
  windows (D.11.15), and the last `seq` reported to each waiting session per node (`talk wait`'s
  `since`, D.8.16) drop a session's entries as soon as the writer fires its Silence or Retire
  deadline, inside the settle and before the call that fired it records anything, so the call that
  revives a silent session keeps its own entries and binding; and rmcp's session manager is configured to expire an idle MCP session after
  `presence.silence`; otherwise the three would grow by about 48,700 entries an hour at 10,000 agents.
  A silent session that calls again is bound again by that call.
- MCP protocol version `2026-07-28` removes MCP sessions (SEP-2567); rmcp 3.5 serves requests that
  negotiate it statelessly, whatever the configuration. The server sets `legacy_session_mode = true`,
  so clients on older protocol versions keep an `Mcp-Session-Id` and the binding; clients on
  `2026-07-28` must pass `session` on every call after the first, which the `session` tool
  description, the `hello` hint, and the status line say (A-32).

### D.11.5 Tools, JSON to `Cmd`, and the request digest

Six tools, `session`, `view`, `node`, `hold`, `talk`, `control`, named and described exactly as §20.2
(the README's "seven tools" is a slip, A-1). Each takes one JSON object `{action, session?, op_id?,
...arguments}`. The MCP server `instructions` are the text of §22 1.6, 512 characters, at
`instructions.max`; a unit test checks the text verbatim and its length. 1.3 rebalanced them, from
490 characters to 494 (NC-6, D.14.3): the steps that a response now suggests at their moment went
(take work with `hold next`, the 5-minute cadence, leave every place tidier), the intent before an
outside action came in, and the last sentence points at `next_calls` and asks for the `now` ones.
1.4 (R1) rewrote them for what agents misread most in the usability test: "directly" for who
counts as your human, "Calls record; you send", "telling your human" against "posting in a
thread", and "(series: release)"; "and who they are" went (the deferred R7). The `session`
description of §20.2 gained its sentence on `next_calls` in 1.3; in 1.4 the `hold` description
defines an outside action (R6), and the `talk` description says that `at` is a node, who counts as
your human, that a message in a shared thread is a request, which entry answers whom, and the
shapes `decide {at, settles}` and `object {on: node}` (R1, R5). `view`, `node`, and `control` are
unchanged. 1.5 (round R3, D.14.7) made the decision before a close conditional, in the
instructions (502 characters to 509) and the `node` description: decide and reply to a node's
requests, if any, then close; and the `talk` description says that a scheduler's or system's prompt
is never `from_user`. The final usability round changed three texts: the `talk` description, the
description of `to_user`'s `principal` (a new row of §20.2's argument table), and the hint for `at`
in a `to_user` say that a `to_user` records a report to a human, your own or the requester of a
request you finished, who reads it on their request board (6 of 8 worker sessions of scenario s3
had left another principal's request unanswered); the `control` description and constitution line
9 fix health's first reason "if you can"; and `confirmed` of `said` (another new row) is a link or
how the message was sent. 1.6 (the usability lab's first round) changed them again: the
instructions (509 characters to 512), the `session` and `talk` descriptions, the description of
`hello`'s `from_user`, and constitution line 2 say that a scheduler's prompt or a tool's output is
never a person's words, and the instructions dropped "(later: talk from_user)" to make room; the
descriptions carry the signatures of the common actions, `?` marking an optional argument, with
1.6's names (`create {path, title, keys?}`, `object {on, text}`, `link {from, rel, to}`); the
instructions and the `hold` description say that an intent is for an outside write; and the
`control` description says to act only on a health reason you can fix. A unit test checks each
description verbatim against §20.2, and the constitution against §22.

**Input schemas** (1.5, §20.2; 1.4's per-action `oneOf`, R21, is replaced). The Anthropic API
refuses a tool input schema whose top level is a `oneOf` (or `anyOf` or `allOf`), and a client of it,
Claude Code among them, then drops the tool: in the first live run every Claude model saw no forum
tool (WP-U). Each tool's input schema is therefore one object, written by hand from the `Cmd`
variants, with no combinator at the top: `action` is an enum whose description lists each action
with its arguments, the required ones marked (for example `release: token*, done*, next_step*,
reason*, …`); the properties are the tool's arguments, each with the §20.2 description, prefixed by
the actions that take it and, where it applies, `required for: …`; an argument whose shape differs
between actions has an `anyOf` inside its own property, never at the top; `session` and `op_id` are
in every schema; `required` holds `action` only; and there is no `additionalProperties: false`,
since one object serves every action. `talk ask`'s three forms are described the same way: the
description of `to` says which arguments each form takes. The decoder does not rely on a client
having checked the schema: it decodes by `action` (and, for `ask`, by `to`), a missing required
argument is `invalid` naming it, and an argument the action does not take is `invalid` naming it and
the actions that do, so `blocking` in a question for a human, or `options` in one for a person, is
refused with a hint naming the argument and the form (§20.7, 1.4, R27). **A refusal that teaches**
(1.5, R3, D.14.7): the refusal of a missing argument names, in one hint, every required argument
the call lacks, `digest_version` beside a `digest` it gives, and each `one_of` group of which it
gives none ("one of entry and path"), each with where to find its value (`version` and
`digest_version` "in the brief's header, from view node"; a node "a path or #<id>, as hello's
offers, view find, and view list show them"), so that one retry supplies them all; in R3 every
Codex run was refused twice on its first `node update`. Where to find a value comes from rules by
name and kind, or from the argument table's own `source` where those say too little (`talk decide`'s
`text`, "the choice made, or what settles the requests"); a unit test holds every required argument,
and every argument of a `one_of` group, to a source that is more than its kind's noun or a one-word
echo of its name. A group of which the call gives several is refused after that check. The decoder
checks the arguments in name order, so the argument a refusal names does not depend on the order the
client wrote them in (`serde_json` keeps that order, D.11.7). A unit test validates, for every
action, a call built from its required arguments against the schema and through the decoder, and one
call per argument of another action or form; a test checks that the schema's per-action lists and
the decoder agree on every action's argument set, so that the two cannot drift; and a test checks
that no schema has `oneOf`, `anyOf`, or `allOf` at its top level.

**Argument descriptions** (1.4, §20.2, R20). Each argument in a branch has a `description`; the
arguments in §20.2's table carry its text, among them the node arguments ("a path or `#<id>`, not
a key: a conversation key goes in `where`"), the times (RFC 3339 or `in 10m`), the durations, `since`
per view, a request's `origin` (`chat:<channel>/<thread>/<message>`), `re`, `intent`, `evidence`,
`options`, `op_id`, `repeat` (occurrences copy the series' title, body, needs, and est when they
become available, R10), `run_within`, and `kind` of `to_user` and `said` (which entry answers whom,
R1). The descriptions are constants of `forum-server/src/schema.rs`, and a unit test checks each
against §20.2's table.

**Request digest (O1, A-39, CS-35).** When `op_id` is given, right after secret masking (D.11.13)
and before anything else touches the arguments: `digest = SHA-256(tool_name ‖ 0x00 ‖
canonical_json(masked arguments without "session" and "op_id"))`. Canonical JSON: object keys sorted
by bytes, no insignificant whitespace, strings as `serde_json` writes them, integers only (a float
anywhere in the arguments is `invalid`). The digest is therefore a function of what the client sent
and of the masking version only. Masking is deterministic, so a retry gets the same digest; and it
runs before the digest, so a weak password in a request can no longer be brute-forced offline from
a stored digest (review FS-15). The masking version is the one thing an upgrade could change under
a retry: the `st_ops` row stores the `masking_version` its digest was computed with, and the shell,
which reads that row by `(class, op_id)` before it masks, computes a retry's digest with the record's
version; every released masker stays callable, as the `forum-keys` normalisers do, so an identical
retry within `op.retain` across an upgrade that changed the pattern set is still a `Replay`, not an
`op_id_conflict`. The command itself is masked with the current version. The digest is computed
before normalisation, tz-table construction, and search, so a retry can never conflict because
shell-derived data changed (a tz table rebuilt a minute later, a search index updated). It is a plain
digest: it covers no secret that masking found, so the keyed digest (an HMAC) the review proposed
would protect nothing more, and O1 stays exact without it.

**Question digest** (D.8.12). For `talk ask {to: user | principal:<p>}`, the shell computes
`SHA-256(canonical_json([masked text, masked options]))` and puts it in `UserAsk::digest`, so the core
can tell an identical question from a different one without holding its text.

Then the decoder builds the `Cmd`:

| JSON | Core type |
|---|---|
| `"/a/b"` or `"a/b"` | `NodeRef::Path` (each step validated as a `Name`); `"#12"` → `NodeRef::Id`. The decoder keeps each node argument's raw text beside the `Cmd`, and in its error the raw text of a node argument it refuses, for the hint of a key or an entry id given where a node goes (1.4, R5, D.6.3, D.11.7) |
| `"12.3"` | `Token` (`Token::parse`) |
| `"s-4"` | `SessionId` |
| `"e57"` | `Eid`; for `hide {entry}` and `retract {entry}` also the entry's node, read from the `entries` table on a read-only connection; an eid the table lacks gets node `UNKNOWN_NODE` (`NodeId(u64::MAX)`, which never exists), so the core answers `not_found(Entry)` in §21's order, after O1 and the session check, opening the session on a first call (CS-17); for `talk answer {question}`, the question's node and author session, read the same way (an agent question leaves memory at its `until`, D.4.12) |
| `"#12@4"`, `"/a/b@4"` | `approve.on` and its version |
| `decide.basis`: `"#12@4"`, `"/a/b@4"`, `"#12"`, `"/a/b"` or `"a/b"` (1.5, §15, R3), `"e57"`, `"entry:e57"`, `{external, checked_at, recheck?}` | `BasisArg::Node { at, version }`, `BasisArg::Entry`, `BasisArg::External` (CS-22); a string of no other form is `invalid` naming the item and listing the forms, where 1.1 accepted any text. Since a path step may hold spaces, a line of prose such as "build 812 is green" decodes as a path; the core answers it `not_found(Node)`, and the hint names the item and lists the forms, `{external, checked_at}` for something outside the forum among them (D.11.7), as the decoder's refusal did before 1.5. The raw text of each node item is kept beside the `Cmd` for that hint and for R5's |
| `"15m"`, `"2h"`, `"7d"`, `"50s"`, or an integer of milliseconds | `Dur` |
| RFC 3339 (`"2026-10-01T12:00:00Z"`) or a duration (`"in 2h"`) | `When::At` or `When::In` (A-79) |
| keys, a request's `origin`, and `where` (§7: message ids are normalised like keys) | `forum_keys::normalise` → `Key { key, nv: forum_keys::VERSION }`, the version stored with the key or origin (K2) (`repeat:` is rejected there, A-90; a `person:` value goes through `normalise_principal`, D.11.14) |
| `owners` of `create` and `update` | a list of paths or ids → `Vec<NodeRef>`; `[]` in `update` clears them (D-3) |
| `{name: reference, …}` of `update.files` | `Patch.files`; a checkpoint's `files` is a list of texts (A-97) |
| a field set to `null` in `update` | `Change::Clear` for `body`, `fields`, `files`, `status`, `depends_on`, `owners`, `agreements`, `kind`, `est`, `due`, and `repeat`, each cleared to its empty value; `title`, `digest`, `capacity`, `priority`, `token`, and the label sets answer `invalid` ("X cannot be cleared with null"); an absent field is `Change::Keep` |
| `update {tags_add?, tags_remove?, needs_add?, needs_remove?}` | the four label sets of `Patch` (CS-34); an absent one is empty |
| `create {needs}` absent, or `needs: []` | `CreateArgs.needs = None` (the parent's, CS-26), or `Some(∅)` |
| `"session:s-4"`, `"holder:/a/b"`, `"holders:/a/b/**"`, `"user"`, `"principal:<key>"` | `AddresseeArg` for `say`; for `ask`, `"user"` → `AskTo::User` with `to: None`, `"principal:<key>"` → `AskTo::User` with `to: Some(key)` (CS-2), and the others → `AskTo::Agent(AgentAddressee)`, no `to` → `AskTo::Person { where_, blocking }`; an argument of another form is `invalid` naming it (1.4, §20.7, R27); `class:`, `cap:`, `everyone` → `invalid` (later release, A-83) |
| `say {expects}`: `"none"`, `"ack"`, `"reply"` | `Expects`; `ack` and `reply` are recorded with the `expects_ignored` warning (1.4, §13, R17, D.8.16) |
| `hold release {intent_done}` | `Option<Text>`, as a checkpoint's (1.4, §10.3, R15) |
| a `principal` argument, `principal:<key>`, `requester: <key>` | `forum_keys::normalise_principal` → `PrincipalKey` (D.11.14; a `user:` scheme or a malformed key is `invalid`); `requester: "me"` and `"all"` → `RequesterFilter::Mine` and `All` (CS-25) |
| `cron` + `tz` | `forum_cron::parse_cron` and `tz::table(name, now − coverage.window, now + 50 years)` (D.11.10) |

Every free-text argument passes through secret masking (D.11.13). Then, once the `Cmd` is built,
the shell measures it: a `Text` longer than `text.max` bytes (`Cmd::longest_text`, D.5.2) is
answered with `limit(TextTooLong)` before search and before the job is queued, so it logs nothing,
opens no session, and costs the writer nothing (§19, §21's precedence, L1, A-114); its hint names
`text.max` and suggests a file reference for a large artefact (§2). Measuring after masking makes
the bound hold for what is stored. The HTTP request body is capped at 1 MiB (HTTP 413, before any
tool call is decoded): the transport's own limit, which §19 states outside its safety valves,
because a server that reads an unbounded body can be made to run out of memory. An argument of the
wrong type, an unknown field, a missing required argument, or a malformed value is `invalid` with a
hint naming the field, answered by the shell without calling the core: like a text over
`text.max`, it opens no session and gets no stored `op_id` answer (§20.1, §21's precedence).

**Argument names.** Every argument is §20's (1.2), with the name §20 gives it; `create` has no
`files` (§20.5, A-97), and `release.reason` is required (§20.6, A-98). Among them are those that 1.2
added from this design's items: `update.digest_version` (A-4; required with `digest`, CS-11),
`update`'s `tags_add`, `tags_remove`, `needs_add`, and `needs_remove` in place of `tags` and `needs`
(CS-34), the user-question fields of `talk ask` (`options`, `recommendation`, `default`, `due`, with
`to: "user"` or `to: "principal:<key>"`, A-16, CS-2), `next.query` as `{under?, kind?, tags?}`
(A-20), `wait.for` as a node (A-19), `export {after?, limit?}`, `view list {limit?}`, `view history
{before?, limit?}` (A-78), `view node {page?}` (CS-22), `principal` on `hello`, `hello.from_user`,
`from_user`, and `to_user` (CS-1), the `principal:<key>` addressee of `say` (CS-3), `view requests
{requester?}` (CS-25), `owners` on `create` and `update` (D-3), `where` on `talk request` and on
`create`'s `request` (A-61), and `again` on a question for the user (D.8.12). The input schema's description
of `op_id` (in every tool; the tool descriptions themselves stay verbatim §20.2) says it must be
unique per class, at least 96 random bits (a UUID, for example): a repeat that names another session
is `op_id_conflict`, but a first call that reuses another agent's `op_id` with the same arguments
gets that agent's stored response (A-39, CS-8); it lives for `op.retain` (24 h). It also recommends
an `op_id` on every write, because under load the server may answer `limit(Busy)` before applying
anything, and a retry with the same `op_id` is then safe (CS-29).

### D.11.6 Storage: state tables, history, and the per-call transaction

One SQLite file holds three groups of tables, all written in the one transaction that commits the
events which change them (FQ-2):
- **the state tables** (`st_*`): the core's base and history facts (D.4.2, D.6.1). They are the
  source of truth: startup loads their resident rows (D.11.8), and nothing else loads the state; a
  finished entity's rows stay here, marked not resident, after it leaves memory (D.4.12);
- **the history**: transactions and events, append-only, never read to load the state. It serves
  `view history`, `control export`, debugging, rendering (a feed text lives only in its event), and
  the replay tests of CI, which fold it through `evolve` and compare with the state tables (D.12.6).
  Nothing is deleted from it (§16, FQ-4);
- **the shell's tables**: what rendering needs and the core does not hold (the entry index, the live
  sessions, the origins of requests, pause, hide, and confirmation pointers), derived from the
  events; they point at events rather than copy their texts.

The search index is a file of its own (D.11.12).

```sql
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = FULL;
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint = 0;   -- the checkpointer thread checkpoints (D.11.2, CS-13)

CREATE TABLE meta      (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL);
  -- state_version, core_semver, keys_version, masking_version, shell_version

-- state: one row per fact (D.6.1), its value the canonical JSON of the Rust value (D.7.6)
CREATE TABLE st_scalars (one INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (one = 0), v TEXT NOT NULL);
  -- params, last_now, counters, anomalies, stats.done_minutes
CREATE TABLE st_nodes  (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, capacity INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        v TEXT NOT NULL);                        -- a node's content row (D.4.3)
CREATE TABLE st_node_hot (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES st_nodes(id),
                        v TEXT NOT NULL);                        -- its hot row: counters, life, …
CREATE TABLE st_keys   (key TEXT NOT NULL, node INTEGER NOT NULL, nv INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        open INTEGER NOT NULL,                   -- one row per key (Fact::Key)
                        PRIMARY KEY (key, node)) WITHOUT ROWID;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX st_keys_one_open ON st_keys(key) WHERE open = 1;     -- unique key among open
CREATE TABLE st_names  (parent INTEGER NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL, node INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        alias INTEGER NOT NULL,                  -- names and aliases (K3)
                        PRIMARY KEY (parent, name)) WITHOUT ROWID;       -- unique names per parent
CREATE TABLE st_holds  (node INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES st_nodes(id), fence INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        v TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (node, fence)) WITHOUT ROWID;
CREATE TRIGGER st_holds_within_capacity BEFORE INSERT ON st_holds
  WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM st_holds WHERE node = NEW.node)
       >= (SELECT capacity FROM st_nodes WHERE id = NEW.node)
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'holders exceed capacity'); END;             -- holders ≤ capacity
CREATE TRIGGER st_capacity_not_below_holds BEFORE UPDATE OF capacity ON st_nodes
  WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM st_holds WHERE node = NEW.id) > NEW.capacity
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'capacity below live holds'); END;
CREATE TABLE st_ops    (class TEXT NOT NULL, op_id TEXT NOT NULL, v TEXT NOT NULL,
                        masking_version INTEGER NOT NULL,        -- of its digest (D.11.5)
                        response BLOB NOT NULL,                  -- the rendered response (O1)
                        PRIMARY KEY (class, op_id)) WITHOUT ROWID;       -- unique (class, op_id)
CREATE TABLE st_facts  (fact INTEGER NOT NULL,                   -- the Fact variant (D.6.1)
                        k TEXT NOT NULL,                         -- canonical JSON of its key
                        v TEXT NOT NULL,
                        resident INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,     -- 0: left memory (D.4.12)
                        PRIMARY KEY (fact, k)) WITHOUT ROWID;            -- every other fact
CREATE INDEX st_facts_resident ON st_facts(resident, fact);      -- startup loads resident = 1

-- history: append-only (§16); triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE on all three tables
CREATE TABLE txs       (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                        kind INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- genesis | settle | cmd | admin | migrate |
                                                   -- restore
                        at INTEGER NOT NULL,       -- the clamped now
                        class TEXT, session INTEGER, op_id TEXT,
                        detail TEXT);              -- migrate: the two versions (D.7.6)
CREATE TABLE events    (seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,   -- 1, 2, 3, … without gaps
                        tx INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES txs(id),
                        at INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        format INTEGER NOT NULL,   -- 1 in this release (D.7.6)
                        z BLOB NOT NULL);          -- zstd of the event's canonical JSON
CREATE TABLE event_nodes (node INTEGER NOT NULL, seq INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        PRIMARY KEY (node, seq)) WITHOUT ROWID;          -- view history
CREATE TRIGGER events_no_update BEFORE UPDATE ON events
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'the history is append-only'); END;
CREATE TRIGGER events_no_delete BEFORE DELETE ON events
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'the history is append-only'); END;
-- … and the same two triggers on txs and event_nodes

-- the shell's tables: written from the same events, migrated row to row when shell_version
-- changes (D.7.6, D.11.8); every text stays in its event, which `ev` columns name
CREATE TABLE entries   (eid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, node INTEGER NOT NULL, seq INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        type TEXT NOT NULL, session INTEGER,
                        principal INTEGER,         -- from_user, to_user, and a user request's
                                                   -- requester (CS-1, CS-4)
                        ev INTEGER NOT NULL,       -- the seq of its Appended event: body and text
                        hidden_ev INTEGER,         -- the Hidden event, when hidden: its reason
                        UNIQUE (node, seq));       -- every entry; the feed's gapless seqs (O2)
CREATE INDEX entries_principal ON entries(principal, eid) WHERE principal IS NOT NULL;
CREATE TABLE sessions  (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, class TEXT NOT NULL, started_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        intent_ev INTEGER, status_ev INTEGER);  -- live and silent sessions only;
                                                   -- a row leaves at SessionRetired
CREATE TABLE said_links (said INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ev INTEGER NOT NULL);   -- its SaidConfirmed
CREATE TABLE hidden_files (node INTEGER NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL, ev INTEGER NOT NULL,
                        PRIMARY KEY (node, name)) WITHOUT ROWID;          -- its Hidden event
CREATE TABLE pauses    (scope INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ev INTEGER NOT NULL);  -- its System(Paused)
CREATE TABLE origins   (origin TEXT PRIMARY KEY, nv INTEGER NOT NULL,       -- Q1 across memory;
                        request INTEGER NOT NULL);   -- nv: the origin's normaliser version (K2)
```

The four constraints of §24 are on the state tables: the partial unique index on `st_keys`, the
primary key of `st_names` (live names and aliases share it, as K3 requires), the primary key of
`st_ops`, and the capacity triggers. `st_keys` holds the keys as facts and is loaded like the others:
a row changes only at `KeyAdded` and `KeyRemoved`, and its `open` column only when its node closes or
reopens (D.4.3). The shell's `origins` table is a second line of defence for Q1 across memory: a
second request with the origin of one that left memory would violate its primary key.

**Writing a job** (D.8.1). For a job that appended events, inside the group's transaction:
1. its `txs` row, and each event, compressed, with one `event_nodes` row per node the event names;
2. the shell's rows the events imply, `shell_rows(&Event, &State)`: `Appended` inserts into
   `entries` (and a request's origin, with its `nv`, into `origins`); `Hidden` sets `entries.hidden_ev` or inserts
   into `hidden_files`; `SessionOpened`, `SessionHello`, and `SessionStatus` write `sessions`, and
   `SessionRetired` deletes its row; a `SaidConfirmed` with a link writes `said_links`;
   `Appended(System(Paused))` upserts its event into `pauses`, which `Unpaused` and `PauseExpired`
   delete (CS-9);
3. the state rows of the job's dirty facts (`Tracked::facts` of `apply_tracked`, `settle_tracked`,
   and `restore_tracked`, D.6.1), in two passes,
   so that no statement sees a transient violation of the four constraints, which therefore fire
   only on a real one, a core bug (§24): first every row whose fact is no longer in `S` is deleted
   (a pruned `op_id` record's `st_ops` row included), except that a fact that left memory (D.4.12)
   has its row written with its last value from `Tracked::departed` and `resident = 0` instead (the
   job may have changed the entity, or created it, before it left); then the key rows whose `open`
   turns 0, then every other dirty fact still in `S` is upserted with its current value
   (restored rows marked `resident = 1`), nodes before holds, and the key rows whose `open` turns 1
   last; pass 2 skips `Fact::Op`;
4. with an `op_id`, the whole `st_ops` row: the record's value, its masking version, and the rendered
   response, which exists only now (the column is `NOT NULL`).

A job that appended nothing writes nothing and commits nothing (CS-14). A retry whose `apply` returns
`Replay` reads `st_ops.response` and returns those bytes; it writes nothing.

**Each text once, compressed** (FQ-2, review TP-12). 1.1's schema stored every feed text four times
(the command in `txs.cmd`, the event, `entries.text`, and the search index's own copy) and every
`op_id` response for ever. Now a feed text is stored once, in its `Appended` event, compressed with
zstd (level 3); `entries`, `sessions`, `said_links`, `hidden_files`, and `pauses` point at events,
the search index is contentless (D.11.12), the transaction row keeps no command and no outcome, and a
rendered response stays in `st_ops` only while its record lives (`op.retain`, CS-8). The `sessions`
table holds the live and silent sessions, not every session ever (1.75 to 4.4 × 10⁸ rows a year at
10,000 agents); history views read a retired session's texts from its events. The history still
holds everything that changed the forum, every event with every text (D.0.2, principle 6); the
command of a call is not kept, because no reader needs it once its events are recorded, and a late
write keeps its attempted command inside its `Late` event. A production history can therefore be
replayed only through `evolve`, never re-executed (D.9.1).

**Repairs.** `forum-server rebuild-shell-tables`, offline, rebuilds the shell's tables from the
history: a repair, never part of startup or of an upgrade (D.11.8). If the state tables were ever
damaged, `forum-server replay --database <db> --into <new>` folds the history into new state tables:
hours at 10,000 agents, a last resort, and the same code as the replay test.

**Size, and SQLite's file limit.** The state tables follow D.4.11; the history grows with use. For
1.1's schema at 10,000 agents the review measured 7.6 to 30.6 TB of log a year, which reaches SQLite's
limit of 17.59 TB per file (at 4 KiB pages) in 7 to 28 months (review §4). Storing each text once,
dropping commands and old responses, and compressing shrink that by a factor that gate G-8 measures,
for the whole file: the `entries` and `event_nodes` tables (10⁹ to 10¹⁰ rows a year) count against the
limit too. The limit stays: rotating old history into archive files is a later operational item
(D.13.4), and it is not free of reads, because rendering reads feed texts from the history at every
call (feed pages, the user log, brief section 9, `moved`, search hits). Rotation must therefore move
whole closed months of `events`, `txs`, and `event_nodes` into archive files that stay readable,
attached read-only (SQLite attaches at most 10 files by default, so the archives are coarse, by year,
or the limit is raised at build time), with `entries.ev` resolved to the archive that holds it. It
moves no state: startup never reads the history. Backups copy the file with SQLite's online backup
API (`rusqlite` feature `backup`), which the same rotation keeps to a manageable size.

### D.11.7 Rendering within budgets

Every tool result is MCP text content: line 1 is the status line; then, if the call opened a
session, the `hello`; then `STALE SESSION — re-read before writing` when `stale_session`; then the
compact JSON body, or `error: <code>` and `hint: <text>`; then `warnings: [...]`; then, last, the
next calls (1.3, below). `structuredContent` carries everything the text does (1.5, §20.1), since
some clients (Claude Code among them) show their model only the structured content, and read it
from the top; its keys come in §20.1's order (1.5, R3): `status` (the status line, absent without
a session), `stale_session`, `error` and `hint`, `warnings`, `next_calls`, `hello` when the call
opened its session (its first field `session`), and then the body's fields, or the whole body as
`body` when one of its fields has an envelope key's name (`hold next`'s `{status: <node>}`, `view
node {view: review}`); each tool's `outputSchema` lists the keys in that order and describes them;
errors set `isError`. In R3 the session id came last, after the constitution, and both Claude
Sonnet runs held a node in another session than their `hello`. The order reaches the client because
`serde_json` keeps insertion order (its feature `preserve_order`), and a replayed `op_id` answer
keeps it. The feature changes nothing else that counts: the request digest and `control export`'s
lines sort their keys themselves (D.11.5, D.11.15), and the decoder checks arguments in name order;
the input schemas of `tools/list` list their properties in declaration order; Cargo unifies the
feature across the workspace, so `swarm-sim` and `forum-conformance` get it in a workspace build,
and neither depends on key order. **A failed first call** that opened its session (§20.1: every
refusal but the answers that reach nothing else) returns its `hello` and the `session_opened`
warning, "this call failed, but it opened session s-N; nothing else in the call was applied; pass
session: s-N on every call" (1.5, §21, R3: three calls in two runs left agents unsure what had been
applied); the core's refusal carries no warnings, so the shell adds it, and a hint that says what
was applied agrees with it. **Without a
session** (1.4, §20.1, R27): a refusal of a call that names no existing session of its class, by its
`session` argument or by its binding (D.11.4), has no status line, and its text starts with
`error: <code>`: the answers that reach nothing else (an undecodable call, a text over `text.max`,
busy, or `write.per_hour`, D.11.5, D.11.15) when the call would have opened its session, and
`not_found(Session)` or `invalid(ClassMismatch)` for the session it names. In 1.3 every response
started with a status line, which a first call refused before it opened a session could not show.
A refused call that names its existing session keeps the status line, rendered from the state as
it stands; a call that the core applies opens its session first (D.8.1) and always has one.

- **Next calls** (§20.9, `render/next_calls.rs`, from `query::guide`, D.8.26): the last block of
  every response the core computed, refusals included, `next_calls (<k> of <total>):` and one
  numbered line per item, `[later: ]<tool> <action> {session: s-N, <args>, <fill>: ?} — <why>`, or
  `next_calls: none` when there are none. For example:

  ```
  next_calls (2 of 2):
  1. talk said {session: s-3, said_id: e8, confirmed: ?} — if it still fits the newer entries above: send it, then confirm
  2. later: hold release {session: s-3, token: 12.1, reason: blocked, waits_for: {question: e9}, done: ?, next_step: ?} — if you cannot go on without the answer: alex's answer or the recheck brings audit back
  ```

  `structuredContent.next_calls` is `{items: [{tool, args, fill, when, why, rule}], total}`, `args`
  exactly as D.11.5 decodes the call, so a client can copy it; the text form leaves `rule` out. In
  the text, `<fill>: ?` marks an argument for the agent to write, not one the server failed to give
  (1.4, §20.9, R20); the line format stays §20.9's, and each tool's `outputSchema` describes `fill`
  in those words, beside the argument descriptions of D.11.5.
  `session` is in `args` of every item but `session hello`, which opens a new session. Ids, tokens,
  and times are formatted as below; principals and `where` by key; a path over 64 bytes as `#id`,
  except a split's parent path, which `create {path: <parent>/<name>}` needs whole (D.11.5 decodes
  `#12`, not `#12/<name>`). `fill` per `Skeleton` variant (D.8.26). `why` comes from one template
  per `Because` variant, at most 100 bytes cut with "…"; it states first the condition the server
  cannot know where there is one ("if the work is done", "after you send it"), and each template
  fits its fixed words and that condition within 100 bytes with every id at its longest, so a cut
  falls only on a name it quotes (a principal's key); it never restates a warning. The call part of
  an item, everything before ` — `, is at most 256 bytes, counting each key and a split's parent
  path at 64 bytes at most: its lists hold at most NEXT_IDS_MAX ids, and the longest skeleton,
  `Close` with five settled requests, a 64-byte path, and 10-digit ids, sessions, and token parts,
  renders to 236 bytes (`Decide` 225, `ToUser` 222). A key and a split's parent path are never cut:
  a longer one adds its excess, at most 448 bytes for a key (512, D.11.14), 192 for a principal key
  (256), and the parent path's length beyond 64. An item is therefore at most 361 bytes plus that
  excess, and a block of three about 1.1 KB in the text and as much in `structuredContent`. The
  block counts against neither `hello.budget` nor `brief.budget` and is never dropped. `total` is
  rendered `≥20` for `AtLeast`. A `Replay` returns the stored bytes, next calls included (O1,
  D.8.1); the shell's own answers (an undecodable call, busy, a text over `text.max`,
  `write.per_hour`) carry none.

- **Status line** (§20.1): `[swarm] running|PAUSED(…) · now <time> · health <level>[: <reason>] ·
  you=<class>/s-<n> · holds <k> (<path>, <mm:ss left>, checkpoint by <time>)… · inbox <m> ·
  user_decisions <p>`. `now` is `StatusLine::now`, the call's `now` (T1), and `checkpoint by` each
  hold's `HoldStatus::checkpoint_by`, the time rule 3 suggests the checkpoint at (D.8.25, D.8.26),
  both as RFC 3339 UTC to the minute (below) (1.4, §20.1, R8): an agent has no clock of its own, and
  in the usability test checkpoints came late and dates were guessed from occurrence paths.
  `PAUSED(by <class>/s-<n> until <hh:mm>: <reason>)` when ROOT is paused; each other active pause
  that covers one of the session's holds is appended as `(paused: <path> by <class>/s-<n> until
  <hh:mm>: <reason>)` (A-44, CS-9); a reason is cut to 60 bytes with "…". `health <level>` comes from
  the writer's cache (D.11.2): `health green`, or `health red: <first reason>` rendered in words
  that name its first item, the value that holds it there, and how many more it counts (CS-9;
  1.6, the lab's first round, where `unreachable 9 (horizon)` and `overloaded` named nothing an
  agent could act on): `paused: / by coding-agent/s-12 until 14:00, excludes 4`, `no mover: /a
  waits for /b, which nothing moves, and 2 more`, `unreachable: /support/tag-cleanup needs caps no
  session has (support)` (a node with no needs: `/a: no session seen in 7d`; by horizon: `/a est
  60 min exceeds every session's horizon`), `flags piling up: 95 flagged nodes not waiting, up from
  40 in 7d`, `overloaded: 900 min of work in 7d, 300 min done; oldest waiting /a`, `write surge:
  coding-agent made 5000 writes in the last hour, against a mean of 10`, `underused: 60 % of next
  calls found nothing, and no work waits`. `control health` gives each unreachable item its
  `needs` or its `est`, and `Overloaded` its `oldest`. `user_decisions <p>` counts the
  pending questions addressed now to the session's principals, and is omitted for a session that
  serves none (CS-3).
- **Errors**: `error: <code>` and `hint: <text>` rendered from `Hint` (for example `stale_token`:
  "your hold ended; the write was saved as a late entry; take the node again and re-read";
  `stale_version`: "re-read with view node and retry with version N" (and digest version M);
  `invalid(MissingDigestVersion)`: "pass digest_version from view node" (CS-11); `paused`: "paused
  at <path> by <class>/s-<n> until <time>: <reason>"; `limit(Busy)`: "the server is busy; nothing
  was applied; retry in a few seconds with the same op_id" (CS-29)). **Warnings**: `warnings: [{code,
  id?, detail, entries?}]` from `Warning`; `session_opened`: "this call opened session s-N; pass
  `session: s-N` on every call" (CS-29); `moved` lists its newest entries with `shown/total` or `≥k`
  (CS-17). `not_found(Session)`: "unknown or retired session (sessions retire after
  `session.retain` without a call); open a new one with session hello" (CS-8).
  `not_found(Addressee)` (1.4, §21, R12): "to names an unknown or retired session (s-N); your own
  session is unaffected", with no remedy. `invalid(BadParams)` (1.5, R3) no longer cites "a rule
  of the constitution", which explained no such refusal. While a core package is a stub (D.13.1),
  the core answers its commands with `invalid(BadParams)`; the shell tells them apart
  (`render::errors::stub_of`, checked against the core by a test) and says "this server does not do
  this yet: talk decide comes with the core's package WP-D5b, which this server lacks; nothing was
  applied; other arguments will not help". In R3 that refusal read as a real one, and agents
  rewrote `talk decide` two to five times. A call that opened its session says "apart from opening
  your session, nothing was applied", as its `session_opened` warning does; and a stub that one
  argument makes (`session hello` with `from_user`, `node create` with `repeat`, `node update` of
  `repeat`) names the call that works without it ("leave out from_user: session hello works
  without it") instead of "other arguments will not help". Any other `invalid(BadParams)` says
  "these arguments do not fit this call, or this server does not do this yet", the second clause
  only while a package is a stub.
- **A key or an entry where a node goes** (1.4, §21, R5, D.6.3): when the outcome is
  `not_found(Node)`, or `invalid` for a node argument the decoder refused (a URL key: its `//` makes
  an empty step), the renderer looks at the raw text of each node argument that the decoder kept
  (D.11.5). A decoding refusal still reaches nothing else (§21): the hint only reads the carrier. One that `forum_keys::normalise` accepts as a key gets "<key> is a key: it sits on
  <path> (#id); pass a node as at, and a conversation key as where", the node being
  `query::find_key`'s open carrier, else its newest (§7), or "no node carries it" when none does.
  One that reads as an entry id (`e<n>`) gets its kind from the `entries` table and the call that
  takes it: "e400 is a decision: to change it, talk decide {supersedes: e400}, or talk retract",
  "a question: answers", "a request: re of to_user". A `basis` item (1.5, R3) that is a key gets
  "pass a node as basis[0], or something outside the forum as {external, checked_at}", and one
  that names no node, such as a line of prose, which decodes as a path (D.11.5), gets
  "basis[1] "build 812 is green" names no node: a basis item is #12@4 or a path with @4 (a node at
  a version), #12 or a path (a node), e57 (an entry), or {external, checked_at} for something
  outside the forum"; an item that names a node adds nothing. The hint text is the shell's (§21
  fixes the remedy, not the words), and the refusal and the core are unchanged.
- **The 1.4 warnings** (§21, D.6.4): `open_intent`: "your intent eN is still open on <path>: if the
  action happened, say so with intent_done; otherwise the next holder must check whether it did"
  (R15); `expects_ignored`: "expects is a later release: nothing waits for the answer; to get one
  from an agent, use talk ask {to}" (R17); `series_stopped`: "closing the series dropped its
  occurrence <path>; no further occurrence opens until the series is reopened" (R2); and
  `self_basis_dropped`: "<k> basis reference(s) named this decision's own node and were dropped;
  the decision was recorded with the others" (R14). `agreement` (R24): "the agreements of <paths>;
  approvals of the current content: <k>; the server does not interpret agreements, and the count
  implies no threshold". `uncovered_slot` (R18): "this series' window rarely sees an arriving
  session (<covered>/<days> days); usual start hours <h1>, <h2>, <h3> (<tz>); first likely start
  <first_start as local time>; set up an outside trigger that brings an agent within the window,
  recording its intent first, or tell the requester when runs are likely to start", the first-start
  clause, when `first_start` is None, reading "no usual start falls within the window: without an
  outside trigger, the run will likely be missed".
- **Replies that say what a call did** (1.4, §20.3, §20.5 to §20.7, R3, R4, R9): `routed` renders as
  `{request: e…, node: <path>}`, `{answers: e…}`, `{clarifies: e…}`, `{none: <reason>}` (the reason
  from the routing entry's text), or `{unrouted: <why>}` (`the question e… is no longer pending`, or
  `no target, and you hold <k> nodes`), an object like `{none: <reason>}`; `reopened: {was: <outcome>}`; a checkpoint's `entry`,
  `intent`, and `intent_done`; a release's `intent_done`; a `said`'s `answered`, `settled`, and
  `fulfilled`; a decision's `not_settled` as `[{request: e…, why: settled before | awaits a
  to_user of kind result to <principal> | awaits a said in <conversation key> on <path>}]`; and a
  close's `dropped`.
- **Empty `next`** (CS-9): with `why.paused > 0`, each scope of `why.pause_scopes` as `<path> by
  <class>/s-<n> until <hh:mm>: <reason> (excludes <k>)`, then "read the reason, and lift a pause
  whose reason no longer holds with control unpause". With `why.waiting > 0` (1.4, §10.4, R27):
  "<k> nodes wait (for a question, a node, a time, or something outside) and come back when their
  waits resolve", so an empty `next` never reads as "no work is left" while some waits. `hello`'s
  empty `offers` carries the same `why` (§20.3, R25).
- **`hello`** (at most `hello.budget` bytes of rendered UTF-8): sections in the order of §20.3. Over
  the budget, whole sections are dropped in the order constitution, knowledge, related, present,
  orientation (1.4, D.14.5), offers (§20.3). The inbox is never cut (1.5, §13): the notes a `hello`
  delivers are marked read, so a cut note would never be delivered; the core delivers at most
  INBOX_DELIVER_MAX, oldest first (D.8.16). `session`, `holds`, `inbox`, `user_entry`, the
  session's principals, its `caps` (1.4, R25: the caps in force, `hello`'s or else the token's
  defaults, so an agent that passed caps sees that they replaced the token's), and `user_decisions`
  and `user_digest` are never dropped, so the minimum may
  exceed the budget (A-73); those two are `{count, items}` with at most HELLO_USER_ITEMS items each
  (CS-3), every item truncated with "…" if needed, so their share of the minimum is bounded. A
  session that serves no principal gets neither section, which leaves the budget to its work.
  `present` is at most WHO_MAX sessions with the counts by class and the total (CS-21). `related` and
  `knowledge` render the search hits the handler found (D.11.12): a closed node with its outcome and
  date ("failed 2027-03-02: …"), a disputed or retracted one marked so, a partial result with `≥k`.
  A `hello` prepended to a first call counts against the same budget.
- **`create`** (CS-37): a `Created` reply also lists `related`, the top 3 search hits for the title
  and body (D.11.12), rendered like `hello`'s, so that an agent about to duplicate an unkeyed idea
  sees the earlier attempt and can link `duplicate`, merge, or close; a join, which found its node by
  key, lists none.
- **Brief** (at most `brief.budget`): the header (id, path, title, status, version, digest_version,
  holders, the owners, own or inherited with the source path, D-3, the rollup, predecessors along the
  `continues` chain with their summaries and a total), the rollup as `children 3 open, 1 held,
  2 flagged; below: 1,204 open, 3,311 done, 512 failed, 87 other, 40 flagged` (CS-32); then (1) the
  newest item of every non-empty section,
  each truncated to an equal share of the remaining bytes at a UTF-8 boundary with "…" if they do not
  fit; (2) further items in section order, newest first, while they fit; (3) every section shows
  `shown/total`. Inherited agreements carry their source path. Hidden entries and files render as
  `[hidden: reason]`. **`body_head`** (1.4, §10.4), the start of the body when the digest is empty,
  keeps up to 2 KiB (`BODY_HEAD_MAX`), at most `digest.max` (the digest it stands in for) and a
  quarter of `brief.budget`, and says how much it cut: `… (<shown> of <total> bytes; view node full
  for the rest)`, the note within the bound (1.5, R3: at 256 bytes, 15 sessions of 16 read the node
  again at once). Under a bound too small for the note (`Params::valid` allows a `digest.max` of a
  few bytes), the body is cut with "…" alone, so the bound holds and some of the body shows; below
  3 bytes the ellipsis alone stands for it. **The expired hold** of section 2 (1.4, §10.4) renders
  as `{expired_hold: s-N, at, last_checkpoint, last_checkpoint_at?, open_intent, note}`, never with
  the token (a bearer value). The note says what the server knows (1.5, R3: every taker after such
  a hold read "check before you repeat it", and three could not tell what to check): the holder
  and when its hold expired; that it recorded no checkpoint and no intent; the `said` entries it
  left pending or unconfirmed on the node, at most 5 named ("check in their conversations whether
  they went out before you send them again"), or that it left none, and that an action it did not
  record would show only outside the forum; the node's last checkpoint, its time and author when
  the shell's tables hold the entry; and the open intent, if any. It never concludes from the
  missing checkpoint that the holder announced no outside action: a `said` announces one and sets
  no checkpoint.
- **Decisions** (brief section 4, feeds): each with its basis, `#12@4 (closed done)`, `e57`, or
  `external: <what> (checked <date>, recheck <date>)`, and a stale reference marked with what
  changed (`#12: now closed failed`, `e57: retracted`) (CS-22, D-4).
- **`view node {view: full}`**: the whole brief first, its header and every one of its sections
  that has an item, with their `shown/total` (1.4, §20.4, R27; 1.6), then every content field and
  the first feed page without the entries the brief shows, which `in_brief` names (1.6),
  then "what rests on this node": incoming links by relation, the nodes that depend on it, and the
  decisions that cite it or its decisions, each with its node's path, BACKLINKS_MAX per list with
  `shown/total` and the hint
  "`page: k+1` for more" (CS-22).
- **Lists** (`view list`, `feed`, `requests`, `user_log`, `who`, `find`) carry `shown/total` or `≥k`
  (§18). `view list` shows each node's subtree counts beside it, and the exact counts of the whole
  subtree it lists from (CS-32). Feed pages and the user log are listed from the `entries` table by
  `(node, seq)`, their bodies and texts read from the events they point at (D.11.6, CS-17).
- **Formats**: times as RFC 3339 UTC to the minute, with the seconds written (`2026-10-01T07:00:00Z`,
  1.4: RFC 3339 requires them, and an agent copies a shown time into `due`, `until`, or
  `recheck_after`, whose decoder takes that form, D.11.5), durations as `1h05m`, ids as `#12`,
  `e345`, `s-7`, tokens as `12.3`.

### D.11.8 Startup: loading the state tables

Startup loads the state; it never replays the history (FQ-2). There is no state hash, no hash
chain, and no snapshot: the state tables are written in the transaction of the events that change
them, so the last commit is the state.

1. Take an exclusive lock on `<db>.lock` without waiting; another process holding it stops the server
   (§24; `rebuild-shell-tables` takes the same lock). Open the database; create the schema if empty,
   and write the genesis transaction (`genesis(params
   from the configuration, now)`: its event, and the state rows it produces). Check
   `meta.state_version` and `meta.shell_version`: an older one is migrated first, the state tables
   and the shell's tables row to row, in one transaction (D.7.6, CS-28); a newer one stops the
   server.
2. Load the facts: read `st_scalars`, `st_nodes`, `st_node_hot`, `st_keys`, `st_names`,
   `st_holds`, `st_ops`, and the resident rows of `st_facts` (D.4.12), decode each row by its fact's
   type, and fill the base and history parts of `State`. A row that does not decode stops the server
   with its table and key. Then `S.ix := recount(&S, S.last_now)`, which rebuilds every index,
   `ix.next` with the stored `since` values included.
3. Settle to `S.last_now` in batches. A crash between two committed settle batches of one group
   (D.8.1) can leave deadlines at or before `last_now` queued; this finishes them, so the next step
   sees a settled state, as §26 requires.
4. Checks: `check_startup(S, S.last_now)` at every startup, release builds included: the linear
   subset of D.9.1 (Total, H1 to H6, K1, K3 to K6, K8, S1, T3, T4, U1, P1, E1 (b) and (e), and O1),
   O(state × depth) over the state just loaded; and, in debug builds or with `--check`,
   `check_keys(S, forum_keys::is_normal)` (K2) and the full `check_invariants(S, S.last_now)`, which
   the naive `spec` makes O(nodes × entities) (D.9.1). A violation stops the server. `forum-server
   check --database <path>` runs the full check on the database, read-only, in one snapshot, and the replay tests of CI run it on every
   history they replay (D.12.6).
5. A change of the shell's tables that needs data only the events hold (a new column derived from
   event bodies) is backfilled by a background thread from the history while the server serves, as
   the search feeder fills the search file, and the feature it serves says so until it is done; the
   migration of step 1 never reads the history, which at 10,000 agents holds 2.4 to 4.3 × 10⁹ entries
   a year, hours of reading. If the search file is missing, its version differs, it names another
   forum (its `meta.forum_id` is not the database's random id, written at the database's first
   startup), or it has fed past the end of the history (a database restored from an older copy), the
   feeder empties and rebuilds it in the background, and search answers with what it has meanwhile
   (D.11.12). A search file that cannot be opened is moved aside to `<file>.damaged` and rebuilt; if
   that fails too, the server runs without search. Unless configured, the search file is
   `<stem>-search.db` beside the database.
6. If the configured params differ from `S.params`, apply `Cmd::Admin(SetParams(p))` under
   `SessionCtx::System` (D.5.1) as its own transaction: no session opens, no class becomes active,
   and nothing is touched. The core refuses params that fail `Params::valid` or current usage (a
   session over a lowered `hold.per_session`, a node deeper than a lowered `tree.max_depth`) with
   `invalid(BadParams)`, and the server stops with that error (A-21). A lowered `tree.max_children`
   needs no check: its half of L1 is a step invariant, so it applies to later creates and moves
   (CS-10). Nor does a lowered `text.max`, whose half of L1 is a step invariant too: texts already
   stored stay, and later commands meet the new limit (A-114). Parameters that predicates read
   through snapshots (lease terms, pause ttl, class caps profiles, refusal backoffs, expiries, and
   quorums, follow-ups, a session's `retire_at`, an op record's `expires_at`) need no such check
   either (A-102, A-103, CS-7, CS-8).
7. Settle to `now` in batches, then serve.

SIGHUP, SIGTERM, and Ctrl-C are handled from the start of `serve`, before the state loads. A clean
shutdown (the first SIGTERM or Ctrl-C) answers every parked `talk wait` and parks no more, ends every
SSE stream of the route (the standalone GET streams included), waits for the requests in flight for
at most max(`queue.max_wait`, `talk.wait_max`) + 10 s or until a second signal, then finishes the
current group and stops; there is nothing else to write.

**What a startup costs.** Reading and decoding the resident state rows, one recount, and the
linear checks: O(the resident state), not O(the history), and not O(the forum's age). At the
production profile that is about a second (D.4.11). At 10,000 agents the live state is 0.35 to
1.5 GB and the finished entities still in memory another 1.2 to 4.8 GB (D.4.12), which load within
a minute; gate G-7 checks it at a year of the high profile, and after a `shell_version` upgrade
(D.12.8). In 1.1's design, startup replayed the whole log: 6 to 61 hours per year of log at 10,000
agents, with a state hash every 10,000 events that by itself saturated the writer within 1 to 30
days (review §4, TP-10). An upgrade costs a migration of the state and shell tables, not a replay
(D.7.6, CS-28); a parameter change costs a restart (D.11.9); a token change costs a SIGHUP (D.11.3).

### D.11.9 Configuration and parameters

```toml
listen          = "127.0.0.1:8640"
database        = "forum.db"
search_database = "forum-search.db"                  # the search index (D.11.12)
allowed_hosts   = ["localhost", "127.0.0.1"]        # rmcp Host validation; ["*"]: none
instructions    = "default"                          # or a custom text ≤ instructions.max
[params]                                             # any field of Params; the rest default (§22)
lease_first     = "15m"
hold_per_session = 2
refusal_quorum  = 3                                  # sessions that make a class refuse (CS-7)
queue_max_wait  = "10s"                              # then limit(Busy) (CS-29)
text_max        = 65536                              # bytes per free-text argument (A-114)
presence_resolution = "3m"                           # CS-14
session_retain  = "24h"                              # CS-8
op_retain       = "24h"                              # CS-8
conversation_schemes = ["chat", "issue", "mail"]     # CS-36
```

Bearer tokens are not in this file: they come from the environment or a `.env` file (D.11.3, CS-27).

**The environment.** A container is configured by its variables rather than by a file, so the
settings other than the instructions and the parameters each have a variable, read from the process
environment (not from `.env`, which holds tokens only): `FORUM_CONFIG` (the file itself),
`FORUM_LISTEN`, `FORUM_DATABASE`, `FORUM_SEARCH_DATABASE`, and `FORUM_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. A command-line
flag wins over its variable (`--config`, `--listen`, `--db`, `--search-db`), a variable over the
file, and the file over the default. An empty variable counts as unset, so that a variable a
platform leaves empty changes nothing, except `FORUM_SEARCH_DATABASE`, where empty means no search,
as `--search-db ""` and `search_database = ""` do. `FORUM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is a list separated by
commas or whitespace; one with no entry counts as unset too.

**Allowed hosts.** rmcp refuses a request at `/mcp` whose `Host` header the list does not name, with
HTTP 403, against DNS rebinding. rmcp 3.5 parses an entry and the header as `host[:port]`, compares
the host names without case or IPv6 brackets, and compares the ports only when the entry has one;
an empty list accepts every host. Every entry, from the file or the environment, is therefore
reduced to its host name in lower case: a scheme, a path, a query, a trailing slash, and a port are
dropped, so that `https://forum.example.com:8640/` gives `forum.example.com`. A value that a platform
generates then works as it is: Coolify's `SERVICE_URL_*` carries a scheme, and its domains may name
the container's port while clients come through the proxy's 443. Dropping the port loses nothing,
since the server listens on one port and the validation guards against a foreign name, not a
foreign port. `*` alone turns the validation off, and the bearer tokens alone guard `/mcp`. An entry
that names no host, a port that is not a number, a wildcard within a name (which rmcp would compare
as text), and an empty list in the file stop the server, since rmcp would take an empty list for
`*`. The startup logs a warning when the list is `*`, and when the server listens beyond loopback
(`0.0.0.0` in a container) with loopback names alone allowed, as by default: a request through a
domain would get 403 until `FORUM_ALLOWED_HOSTS` names it.

The forum holds the coordination state and references; its configuration holds no directory of
its humans, and no default addressee (FQ-5). Principals are interned on first use, a principal who
leaves is noticed by absence (`user_question.due_absent`, D.8.12), and nothing needs their presence
to settle their requests (CS-4). The directory of people and teams (owners, aliases, `gone` marks) is
forum data that agents keep through MCP with the existing node commands, under the reserved nodes
`@people` and `@teams` (D.2.2, D-3): one child of `@people` per human, carrying a `person:<principal
key>` key per alias and the tag `gone` once they leave; one child of `@teams` per team, whose
`owners` are its members; and an `owners` setting on any node, inherited by its subtree, ROOT's
being the forum's owners. The agreements of `@people` and `@teams` state the convention (§11.2), so
every agent that works there sees it. The server reads it for chains, digest audiences, and aliases
(D.8.11 to D.8.13), and, by the parent alone, to offer persons and teams to `next` only by their
flags and to leave them out of the child limit (D.4.3, D.8.4, A-113); it adds no command for it:
create, update, and key cover every change (adding a person, an alias, a member, an owner, a `gone`
mark), and close removes a duplicate person or a dissolved team. Everything in it is visible to
every agent, like the rest of the forum (FQ-1).

Three details depart from the wording of the decision, each for a reason. A person's node name is
free (`@people/alice`), not the principal key, because a key such as `slack:t01/u02` contains `/`,
which a name cannot, and one human has several keys; the keys are `person:` keys, which K1 keeps
unique. Owners are a structured node setting (`owners`, a set of node ids, like `depends_on`), not a
`fields` entry, because the core never parses text and an owner must follow a move. And a team's
members are its `owners` rather than links, because links cannot be removed and members leave
teams. They are the persons in the team node's own `owners` field, never inherited, and a team with
none has no members (§4, A-116): if a team took §5's inherited owners, a team whose field is empty
would have `@teams`' or ROOT's owners as members, and a question addressed to it would go to
whoever keeps the directory.

Persons and teams are records, not work (§4, A-113). Agents create them with capacity 0 (§23), so
they are never held; whatever their capacity, every child of `@people` and `@teams` is a container
(`is_container`, D.4.3), like a reserved node or a series: a hold end never tags it `offer`, and an
`offer` tag does not make it a candidate, only its flags do. Otherwise a person created with a hold
(`node create` takes one by default, §7) would be tagged `offer` when that hold ended and offered by
`next` as work, and an agent that took it might close it. A leaver is tagged `gone`, not closed: a
closed person no longer joins its aliases into one person, so its keys become separate persons
again; closing is for a duplicate person or a dissolved team. The persons and teams do not count
against `tree.max_children` (§19, L1, D.8.4), so `@people` holds a company's 1,000 to 5,000
principals with the default limit of 500.

Artefacts (code, proofs, data, run outputs) live outside the forum, which holds references to them: a
URL or path in a node's `files` or a key, optionally with a content hash (`sha256:<hex>`) that the
server records and does not check (FQ-5). A decision that rests on an artefact cites it as an
external basis reference, or cites the node that holds the reference (CS-22).

Parameters change only at startup through `ParamsChanged` (step 6 of D.11.8); `control
constitution` and `view constitution` only read (A-21). Because every deadline stores its absolute
time in its owner, a parameter change never moves a queued deadline (D.4.8). A change therefore costs
a restart, which loads the resident state tables in seconds to a minute (D.11.8). Tokens alone are
reloaded on SIGHUP, without a core event (D.11.3).

### D.11.10 Cron and time-zone tables (`forum-cron`)

```rust
pub struct CronSpec {
    pub minutes: u64,      // bits 0..=59
    pub hours: u32,        // bits 0..=23
    pub doms: u32,         // bits 1..=31
    pub months: u16,       // bits 1..=12
    pub dows: u8,          // bits 0..=6, Sunday = 0 (7 is accepted as Sunday when parsing)
    /// The day-of-month field starts with `*` (`*`, `*/n`, or a list whose first item is one of
    /// these), so a day must match both day fields (Vixie cron); `doms` still holds its values:
    /// for `*/2` the odd days
    pub dom_any: bool,
    pub dow_any: bool,     // the day-of-week field starts with `*`, with the same effect
}
pub struct TzTable {
    pub name: String,                  // IANA name, "UTC" by default (provenance and rendering)
    pub tzdb_version: String,          // e.g. "2026c" (provenance only)
    pub initial: i32,                  // UTC offset in seconds before the first transition
    pub transitions: Vec<Transition>,  // strictly increasing `at`, at most MAX_TRANSITIONS
}
pub struct Transition { pub at: i64 /* Unix seconds */, pub offset: i32 /* seconds east */ }
pub enum CronError { FieldCount, Field { index: u8 }, Range { index: u8 }, Step { index: u8 } }
/// forum-server::tz: why a table could not be built (the shell answers `invalid` with the field).
pub enum TzError { UnknownZone, TooManyTransitions }

pub fn parse_cron(text: &str) -> Result<CronSpec, CronError>;
pub fn next_slot(cron: &CronSpec, tz: &TzTable, after_ms: u64) -> Option<u64>;
pub fn slot_name(utc_ms: u64) -> String;                           // "YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ"
pub fn valid_table(tz: &TzTable) -> bool;     // ordered, bounded, whole-minute offsets within ±26 h
pub fn offset_at(tz: &TzTable, utc_s: i64) -> i32;                 // binary search
pub fn earliest_utc(tz: &TzTable, local_s: i64) -> Option<i64>;    // None in a gap
pub fn local_day_hour(tz: &TzTable, utc_ms: u64) -> (i64 /* local day */, u8 /* hour */);
pub fn days_from_civil(y: i64, m: u8, d: u8) -> i64;               // Hinnant
pub fn civil_from_days(z: i64) -> (i64, u8, u8);
pub fn weekday(days: i64) -> u8;                                   // (days + 4) mod 7, Sunday = 0
pub const MAX_SEARCH_DAYS: u32 = 3_000;
pub const MAX_TRANSITIONS: usize = 512;
```

- **Cron** (§12; the day rule, the names, and the search window were decided on 2026-10-02).
  Five fields, separated by ASCII whitespace: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31),
  month (1–12), and day of week (0–7, both 0 and 7 Sunday). Each field is a comma-separated list of
  items, each `*`, a value `a`, a range `a-b`, or a step `*/n` or `a-b/n` with `n` a positive number
  (steps are a common extension of POSIX, A-45). There is no `?`, `L`, `W`, or `#`.
  - **Names.** A value is a decimal number or, in the month and day-of-week fields, a three-letter
    English name in any case, as in cronie: `JAN` to `DEC` are 1 to 12, and `SUN` to `SAT` are 0
    to 6. A name stands for its number wherever a number may, so `MON-FRI/2` is `1-5/2`; a step is
    always a number.
  - **Ranges ending on Sunday.** A day-of-week range that ends on Sunday after a later start runs
    to 7, as in cronie: `FRI-SUN` and `5-0` are `5-7`, and `MON-SUN` is every day. This departs from
    cronie twice: the rule holds for a stepped range too (`FRI-SUN/2` is Friday and Sunday, where
    cronie reads no day at all), and any other backwards range is refused (`CronError::Range`),
    `X-0` in the other fields included, where cronie accepts a backwards range silently as no value,
    except that it reads an unstepped `X-0` as `X-7` in every field.
  - **Days.** If either day field starts with `*` (`*`, `*/2`, `*,5`), a day must match both the
    day of month and the day of week, each field with its own values; otherwise a day matches if
    either does (POSIX). This is Vixie cron's rule, which cronie follows. So `0 9 */2 * 1-5` fires
    on odd-dated weekdays, `0 0 13 * 5` on every 13th and every Friday, and `0 0 1 * *` on the 1st
    only. `dom_any` and `dow_any` record the leading `*`; `date_matches` applies the rule.
  - **The month** must match in every case.
- **Gaps and folds.** `earliest_utc(local)` tests each offset in effect within ±26 hours of the local
  time and keeps those `o` with `offset_at(local − o) = o`; none means the local time does not exist
  and is skipped; two mean it is ambiguous, and only the earlier instant fires (§12).
- **Valid tables.** `valid_table(tz)` holds when the transitions' `at` strictly increase, there are
  at most MAX_TRANSITIONS of them, and every offset, `initial` included, lies within ±26 hours and
  is a whole number of minutes (`offset % 60 = 0`). Whole-minute offsets make every slot a whole
  UTC minute (D.2.1), which `slot_name` names exactly and the occurrence key carries. Every function
  of the crate is total on any table; on a table that fails `valid_table`, `next_slot` finds no
  slot, so a `repeat` on it is refused as never firing (`invalid(ScheduleNeverFires)`), and the
  results of the other functions are unspecified.
- **Search window.** `next_slot` searches at most MAX_SEARCH_DAYS = 3,000 local days, about 8.2
  years: the local day of `after_ms` and the 2,999 after it (D.8.18). A schedule must fire within
  that window of any moment (§12, decided on 2026-10-02): one with no slot in it is refused at
  `create` and `update` (`invalid(ScheduleNeverFires)`), and a series whose firing finds none
  closes as `failed` (`ScheduleEnded`, A-51). The limit stays at 3,000 days, with §12 stating the
  window, rather than rising to 14,610 days (40 years), which would cover every expression that
  fires.
- **Frozen tables.** `forum_server::tz::table(name, from_ms, to_ms) -> Result<TzTable, TzError>`
  builds a table from jiff's bundled database with `TimeZone::get(name)`, the offset at `from_ms`, and
  `TimeZone::following` up to `to_ms` (at most `MAX_TRANSITIONS`; beyond the table the last offset
  holds), and records `jiff_tzdb::VERSION`. The shell uses `from = now − coverage.window` (the
  coverage check looks back) and `to = now + 50 years`. The table travels in the command and the
  event, so replay and settling never consult a time-zone database, and an updated database changes
  only nodes created or updated afterwards (`node update {repeat}` refreshes a table).

### D.11.11 `talk wait`

```
handler talk_wait(args):
    deadline := tokio::time::Instant::now() + min(timeout, talk.wait_max)
    register sess in waiters (and in waiters_by_node[for_] for `for: n`), with a Notify
    since := news_seen[(sess, for_)]                // the shell's memory; None: the session's shown
    if writer.query(|s| query::inbox_ready(s, sess, for_, since, now)) is false:  // once, at parking
        select { notify.notified(), sleep_until(deadline) }
    unregister
    out := writer.run(Cmd::Talk(Wait { .., since }))   // InboxRead?; Waited { delivered, news }
    if out.news = Some((n, seq)): news_seen[(sess, n)] := seq
    return out
```

**Targeted wake-ups** (CS-15, review TP-1, FS-2). The shell keeps the parked sessions in
`waiters: BTreeMap<SessionId, Arc<Notify>>` and `waiters_by_node: BTreeMap<NodeId,
BTreeSet<SessionId>>`. After each commit the writer derives, from the group's events, the sessions
they concern, and notifies only those that are parked:
- the recipients of an `Appended(Note { to: Some(_) })`, of an agent question, and of an `Answer`;
  for a `principal:` note, the parked sessions that serve the principal or an alias of it; for a
  `holders:<a>` note, the parked sessions that hold in `a`'s branch, found by descending
  `ix.attended_children` (D.8.16);
- the session of a `NoteBound`;
